# The Collectors

## I.

The newspapers lived in the hallway. Three columns, flush against the east wall, organized by date and further subdivided by section—front page, metro, business, arts, sports—each section folded to its original crease and sleeved in a gallon-size Ziploc bag to prevent yellowing from the ambient moisture that crept through the building's old plaster. Margot Kessler could navigate the corridor between the papers and the opposite wall if she turned sideways and led with her left shoulder, which she always did, because leading with the right would bring her elbow dangerously close to the April 2007–September 2008 stack, which had developed a lean.

Beyond the hallway, the apartment opened into a series of negotiations between Margot and her possessions. The living room was not a room but a system. Takeout menus, filed by borough and suborganized by cuisine, occupied the bookshelves that no longer held books because the books had been migrated to the bathtub, which Margot no longer used for bathing because the books needed the dry porcelain, and she had learned to wash herself efficiently at the kitchen sink, which she accessed via a path between the hotel soaps (north wall, eight shelving units, fragrance families: floral, citrus, herbaceous, musk, marine, gourmand, woody, unclassifiable) and the shopping bags (south wall, folded flat, organized by retailer and era, the B. Altman bags being the crown jewels, irreplaceable now, and stored in their own acid-free tissue).

She did not experience this as clutter. She experienced it as a solved equation. Every object had been assigned a coordinate, a justification, a relationship to the objects adjacent. She moved through her apartment the way a librarian moves through stacks: with proprietary grace, with the assurance that the disorder perceived by others was simply a filing system they hadn't been taught. And when the anxiety came—the formless, humming anxiety that had no name and no source and arrived on no schedule—she could quiet it by sorting. By picking up a take-out menu from the unprocessed pile on the kitchen counter and determining its correct location: Thai, Brooklyn, Cobble Hill, still operating (she checked on her phone), therefore active file, shelf three, slot fourteen. The click of the menu sliding into place was a click inside her skull, a tumbler falling, a lock engaging. For a moment the world was shut and sealed and she was safe inside it.

The letter came through the mail slot at 3:47 p.m. on a Tuesday. She heard it land on the hallway floor, the whisper of paper on wood, and her first response was not curiosity but categorization. Envelope, white, standard No. 10, handwritten address, no return address. The handwriting was not immediately familiar. She held it up to the hallway's one bare bulb and saw the shadow of a single folded page inside. She brought it to the kitchen counter—the processing station—and set it next to the other unprocessed mail: two credit card offers (financial, unsolicited, discard pile), a flyer for gutter cleaning (household services, maybe pile), and a postcard from her dentist (medical, action required, tickler file). The letter needed a category before she could open it. Personal correspondence, handwritten, unknown sender. She didn't have a location for that. She stared at the envelope for eleven minutes, turning it over twice, before she slit it with the opener she kept in the utensil drawer between the grapefruit spoons and the melon baller.

The first line she read was: *You have never thrown anything away, so you will understand what it means that I have kept everything.*

Dean Pryor was in the men's department at Nordstrom when it happened. He had a cashmere scarf in his left hand, heather gray, $225, and he was running his thumb along the tag while pretending to examine a display of leather gloves with his right. The security camera was in the upper northeast corner, a smoked half-dome the size of a cantaloupe. He'd clocked it on entry. He'd also clocked the sales associate—mid-fifties, glasses on a beaded chain, currently helping a woman in camel decide between cognac and oxblood in a driving glove—and the secondary exit through the shoe department, and the placement of the anti-theft sensor on the scarf, which was a hard tag, not a strip, which meant he'd need to leave it, except that the tag was attached with a standard pin through a care label, and the care label was sewn with a single stitch of thread that would surrender to a firm, directed tug without damaging the scarf itself.

He did not need the scarf. He made $212,000 a year as a systems architect for a logistics company in northern Virginia. He had fourteen cashmere scarves at home, most of them still in the tissue paper he'd balled them in after pulling the tags. He did not wear scarves. He did not particularly like scarves. What he liked was this: the state between deciding and doing, the four or five seconds when the object was transitioning from theirs to his and the entire sensory world narrowed to a tunnel—his hand, the fabric, the pin, the camera, the associate, the distance to the door—and everything else, every email and errand and mortgage payment and unanswered text from his mother, went silent. It was the closest he came to meditation. His therapist, whom he'd seen for two years and told nothing of consequence, had once suggested he try mindfulness exercises. He had not told her that he'd already found one.

The pin released. The tag dropped to the display shelf. The scarf moved to his interior jacket pocket in a motion so fluid it had no visible beginning or end. He walked to the shoe department and out through the side exit at a pace that was unhurried but not slow, and in the car he sat with the scarf on his lap and felt the warmth of the steal radiating through him like the first sip of whiskey on an empty stomach—a loosening, a permission, a moment of animal well-being—and then it was over, and the scarf was just a scarf, and he was just a man sitting alone in a parking garage with something he didn't want.

His phone buzzed. His neighbor, the retired postal worker who collected his packages when he traveled, had texted a photo: an envelope on his doormat, white, handwritten, the address in a cramped script he recognized slightly and couldn't place, the way you half-recognize a face from a dream.

He enlarged the photo. His neighbor had included the text: *Looked important. Want me to open it?*

Dean stared at the handwriting. Something in his chest shifted—not the warm loosening of a steal but its opposite, a tightening, a pin being driven in.

*No*, he typed back. *Don't touch it.*

When he got home and opened the envelope, the line that surfaced first from the single folded page was: *I know what you take and I know why you take it and I know where it started.*

The Wendy's was on Route 1, the one with the parking lot that faced a drainage ditch rather than the road, which was why April Chandler chose it. She could park with her back to the drive-through lane and be invisible from three of four directions, the fourth being a stand of scrub pines that had never, in the eleven years she'd been coming here, contained another human being. She had a Jr. Bacon Cheeseburger, a Spicy Chicken Sandwich, a ten-piece nugget, a large fry, a large Frosty, a second Jr. Bacon Cheeseburger, and a side salad that she would not eat but that she'd ordered to dilute the rest of the tray, to make it look, if anyone could see her, which they couldn't, as though this were a varied and considered meal rather than what it was, which was five minutes of annihilation.

She ate with efficiency. She did not taste the food in any way that would be recognizable as tasting. Taste was not the point. The point was the fullness, the overcapacity, the moment when her body became so packed with substance that there was no room left for the other thing, the thing she could not name and had never been able to name, the thing that had lived in her chest since she was twelve and felt like a scream that wouldn't come out and wouldn't go back down. The food sat on the scream. The food was a lid. And for the five minutes it took to eat everything on the tray, and the ten minutes after, she was sealed.

Then the seal broke, as it always broke, and she was in the Wendy's parking lot with a backseat full of wrappers and her forehead against the steering wheel, counting backward from one hundred. At seventy-three she opened the car door and spit into the gravel. She would not purge. She'd stopped purging after the second hospitalization, the one with the feeding tube, the one her mother flew in for. She would sit with the fullness and the shame and she would wait for her body to process it and she would drive home and she would put the wrappers in a plastic bag and distribute them among three separate public trash cans—the one at the gas station on Maple, the one at the dog park on Birch, the one behind the Rite Aid on Central—because if she put them all in her own kitchen trash, they would form a stratum, an archaeological record of the binge, and anyone who opened the lid would see it and know. No one opened her trash. No one came to her apartment. But she maintained the protocol the way a spy maintains a cover: automatically, religiously, long after the war is over.

When she got home at 7:40, the letter was in her mailbox, its corner bent where the carrier had forced it past a bundle of coupon circulars. She opened it on the front steps because she didn't want to bring an unknown thing inside yet, not while she was still full, not while her defenses were down.

The line that found her was: *I still have the photographs from the night you ate everything on the table while the rest of them dug.*

She read it twice, then folded the letter back into its envelope, put the envelope in her coat pocket, went inside, locked the door, and stood in her dark kitchen for a long time with her hand over her mouth.

Chen Wei was telling the Bourdain story again. He was telling it to a dinner party in a loft in Silver Lake, seven people around a reclaimed-wood table, and he was at the part where Bourdain had leaned over the bowl of *laap* and said, "This is the dish that justified the trip," and Chen had said—

"I didn't say anything at first. I just watched him eat. And I remember thinking: This is a man who experiences food the way I experience music. Total surrender. He closed his eyes."

Chen closed his own eyes to demonstrate. He felt the table's attention tighten around him like a drawstring. This was the drug: not the lie itself but the listening, the moment when a fabricated experience became, through the alchemy of an audience's belief, more real than anything that had actually happened to him. He had never been to Laos. He had never met Anthony Bourdain. He had eaten *laap* once, at a Thai restaurant in Glendale, and it was fine. But the story had been built over six years of telling—each iteration adding a sensory detail, a line of dialogue, a  contextual flourish—until it was a cathedral, load-bearing and intricate, and he lived inside it more comfortably than he lived inside any true thing.

He opened his eyes. The woman across from him, a ceramicist with a gap between her front teeth, was looking at him the way they always looked at him: like he was a window into a more interesting world. He'd fabricated his way into this dinner party, too. The host thought Chen was a documentary filmmaker. Chen was an assistant at a post-production house who logged footage and very occasionally synced audio. But "documentary filmmaker" was the seed that had grown the invitation, and the invitation had grown the Bourdain story, and the Bourdain story had grown this moment of being seen, being envied, being *believed*, and the warmth of it was the warmth that nothing else provided—not money, not sex, not the actual small true life he lived in a studio apartment with a hot plate and a cat named Roger.

He'd told so many lies that the architecture of his identity was entirely decorative, a façade with no building behind it. He sometimes had the feeling that if he stopped lying, he would stop existing—that the lies were not departures from a self but the substance of one, and that beneath them was only the terrified twelve-year-old who'd learned, in one horrible week at a summer camp in upstate New York, that the truth was something that could bury you.

He left the dinner party at eleven. On his hall table, between a stack of film festival programs (he did not attend film festivals) and a vintage Leica (he did not take photographs; the camera was a prop), the letter waited. The envelope was white, handwritten, and postmarked from a town whose name he recognized the way you recognize a scar on your own body—automatically, with a flinch you've learned to suppress.

He opened it standing up, still wearing his jacket, because he already knew what it was, or what category of thing it was. He'd been expecting it for twenty years. Not this exact letter, but a letter. A phone call. A knock at the door. Some vehicle of arrival for the truth he'd been outrunning since he was twelve.

The line that reached him was: *You built a life out of stories, so you'll appreciate that I've built a very good one about you, complete with evidence.*

He read the rest. Then he read it again. Then he picked up his phone and called a number he hadn't dialed in eighteen years, a number he was not entirely sure would work, and when the voicemail picked up—Margot's voice, clipped and careful, reciting her number back as confirmation—he said: "It's Chen.
